en: I praise this lotus-eyed Gaurī, my Mother, whose mass of radiance is equal to a row of rising suns; she who, through her divine play, has established and yet dissolved all worlds, and who is sought for a long time within by world-transcending yogins. || 1 ||

I praise that lotus-eyed Mother Gaurī, who is composed of truth, knowledge, and bliss, who assumes a physical form, and who eternally brings about the pinnacle of liberation within the minds of those established in withdrawal of the senses, meditation, and meditative absorption.

I praise Ambā, the lotus-eyed Gaurī, whose face is graced by a gentle smile that delights Candrāpīḍa, whose mass of dark curls is adorned by Candrāpīḍa, and whose pair of lotus feet are worshipped by Indra, Upendra, and the other gods. || 3 ||

I praise that Mother Gaurī, whose lotus-eyes gaze upon me; she who shines forth as the form of all letters from 'a' to 'kṣa', who gives birth to the multitude of beings in every single being, and who consists of the bliss of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), radiant like a flash of lightning.

I praise that Mother Gaurī, whose lotus-like eyes are the form of bliss, whose body is more subtle than the subtlest, who has traveled through the path rising from the *mūlādhāra* to pervade the *brahmarandhra*—the solar and lunar apertures—and whose limbs blaze with the radiance of her divine play.

I praise Ambā, the lotus-eyed Gaurī, the consort of Śiva, who is eternal, pure, partless, and one; who is the Lord of the universe and the witness to its creation and dissolution; and who delights in the play of protecting the world. 6.

I praise that lotus-eyed Mother Gaurī, who sports with her Lord on the Silver Mountain (Kailāsa), and whose womb contained the entire cosmic egg in its unbroken state, which emerged again and again as soon as it arose.
I praise that lotus-eyed Mother Gaurī, who is to be reached by the path of spiritual knowledge, in whom everything—both moving and unmoving—is woven like a string of jewels upon a thread.

I praise that auspicious Mother Gaurī, the lotus-eyed one, who, though she is herself one, sports at her own will pervading the worlds with various forms and multitudes of powers; she is a wish-fulfilling creeper for those who bow before her.

I praise that Ambā, the lotus-eyed Gaurī, who brings about the destruction of the bonds of hope and the afflictions for those men intent on meditating upon her lotus feet; she is the beautiful mistress who takes half the body of the Lord.

To him who, pure in heart, daily recites this "Ten Verses on Gaurī" with devotion and resolve at the time of dawn, the Daughter of the Mountain will surely grant perfection of speech, supreme prosperity, and devotion to Śiva. (11)

Thus ends "The Ten Verses on Gaurī," composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the wandering ascetic teacher of the supreme order (Paramahaṃsa-parivrājaka-ācārya) and disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavat-pūjyapāda.
